==English==

===Etymology===
From {{der|en|enm|in}}, {{m|enm|inn}}, from {{der|en|ang|inn||a dwelling, house, chamber, lodging}}; akin to {{cog|is|inni||a dwelling place, home, abode}}, {{cog|fo|inni||home}}.

===Pronunciation===
* {{enPR|ĭn}}, {{IPA|en|/ɪn/}}
* {{audio|en|en-us-inn.ogg|a=US}}
* {{rhymes|en|ɪn|s=1}}
* {{homophones|en|in}}

===Noun===
{{wp}}
{{en-noun}}

# Any [[establishment]] where [[traveller]]s can [[procure]] [[lodging]], [[food]], and [[drink]].
#: {{syn|en|Thesaurus:lodging place}}
#* {{RQ:Irving Tales of a Traveller|part=1|chapter=The Adventure of My Uncle|page=21|passage=[H]ow much more agreeable to himself to get into snug quarters in a chateau, [...] rather than take up with the miserable lodgement, and miserable fare of a country '''inn'''.}}
#* {{RQ:Churchill Celebrity|chapter=IV|pages=46–47|pageref=46|passage=One morning I had been driven to the precarious refuge afforded by the steps of the '''inn''', after rejecting offers from the Celebrity to join him in a variety of amusements. But even here I was not free from interruption, for he was seated on a horse-block below me, playing with a fox terrier.}}
# A [[tavern]].
#: {{syn|en|Thesaurus:pub}}
# One of the colleges (societies or buildings) in London, for students of the law barristers.
#: {{ux|en|the '''Inns''' of Court    the '''Inns''' of Chancery    Serjeants’ '''Inns'''}}
# {{lb|en|Britain|dated}} The town residence of a nobleman or distinguished person.
#: {{ux|en|Leicester '''Inn'''}}
# {{lb|en|obsolete}} A place of shelter; hence, [[dwelling]], [[residence]], [[abode]].
#* {{RQ:Spenser Shepheardes Calender|chapter=November|folio=44|verso=1|passage=But nowe ſadde Winter welked hath the day, / And ''[[w:Apollo|Phœbus]]'' weary of his yerely taſ-ke: / Yſtabled hath his ſteedes in lowlye laye / And taken vp his '''ynne''' in ''Fiſhes'' [[hask|haſ-ke]].}}
#* {{RQ:Spenser Faerie Queene|canto=I|book=I|stanza=33|page=12|passage=Therefore with me ye may take vp your '''In''' / For this ſame night.}}

===Verb===
{{en-verb}}

# {{lb|en|obsolete|intransitive}} To take lodging; to [[lodge]] or house oneself.
#* {{RQ:Addison Freeholder|issue=22|date=March 5 1714|passage=But where do you intend to '''inn''' to-night?}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1726|title=Brice's Weekly Journal|section=18 February, 3
|passage=John Welch, Cornish Carrier, who formerly '''Inn'd''' at the Mermaid in Exon, is now removed to the Bear-Inn.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1885|author=M. J. Colquhoun|title=Primes in Indis|section=I, xiv, 217
|passage=I '''inned''' at the best house, the Star and Garter.}}
# {{lb|en|obsolete|transitive}} To lodge or house (someone or something).
#* {{quote-book|en|year=2018|origyear=1607|author=Thomas Middleton|title=Michaelmas term and a trick to catch the old one|publisher=Walter de Gruyter GmbH & Co KG|isbn=9783111392158|page=27
|text=I have but '''Inn'd''' my horse since, master Cockstone.}}
